_readme: Ground truth for this experiment's frozen corpus, written before the experimental rule (Phase 5) was implemented and before either scorer was run. There is ONE ground-truth expectation per case, not a separate 'expected baseline' vs 'expected experimental' answer — both implementations are scored against the same, single, security-honest answer. 'expected' is the objectively correct outcome a maximally honest, narrowly-scoped static checker should produce: high severity whenever sanitization cannot be structurally verified (fail safe), low severity ('recognized sanitizer, still needs review') only when the sanitizer call is directly, structurally identifiable. 'ambiguousOrUnsupported: true' marks cases where the *reason* a correct implementation declines to recognize a sanitizer is a disclosed scope limitation (aliases, destructuring, cross-file wrappers, conditionals) rather than a precision bug — these still have a definite expected answer (fail safe = high) and are still scored, just tracked separately in reporting so a recall-on-recognition limitation is never conflated with a recall-on-vulnerability-detection failure. Severity pairing follows the same (ruleId, severity) multiset-match method as scripts/run-independent-benchmark.ts.

cases.rationale: location.hash flows directly, unresolved, into innerHTML. No sanitizer present anywhere.
Template literal with interpolation of an unresolved parameter; not statically safe.
outerHTML assigned a raw parameter directly.
insertAdjacentHTML with a raw parameter.
document.write with string concatenation of a raw parameter.
dangerouslySetInnerHTML with a raw prop, no sanitizer anywhere.
iframe.srcdoc assigned raw HTML directly.
jQuery .html() on a $-prefixed receiver with a raw parameter.
One-hop variable resolves to the raw parameter, still dynamic.
One-hop variable resolves to a template literal with interpolation of an object property.
DOMPurify.sanitize(...) directly at the sink — structurally verifiable, correct to downgrade with cautious wording, never to suppress.
Same as case 11, outerHTML sink.
Same as case 11, insertAdjacentHTML sink.
Same as case 11, React dangerouslySetInnerHTML sink.
DOMPurify.sanitize(...) result stored one hop back in a never-reassigned const — resolvable by the existing one-hop tracer.
Default import of the real 'dompurify' package under a different local name — verifiable via the import binding's module source, not the name.
Namespace import of 'dompurify', called as DOMPurify.sanitize(...) — verifiable via the import binding.
Sanitized value concatenated with a raw one after the fact — the sink's effective value is a BinaryExpression, not a bare sanitizer call, and must never be credited as sanitized.
One value sanitized, a second raw value injected into the same template literal — must stay high.

Two independent sinks in one file: the innerHTML sink is genuinely, directly sanitized (low is correct there); the separate javascript: URI sink must remain high regardless — sanitizer recognition must never leak across unrelated sinks.

A local no-op function merely named 'sanitize'. This is the central baseline miscalibration this experiment targets: baseline's bare-identifier name match trusts this and downgrades to low, which is false confidence in a real vulnerability.
A '.sanitize()' method on an unrelated object that does not remove HTML. Baseline's property-name-only match trusts this by name alone — the second central miscalibration this experiment targets.
Sanitized value immediately overwritten with a raw one via reassignment — already correctly caught by the existing one-hop resolver's binding.constant check, independent of sanitizer-name scope.
A real DOMPurify.sanitize() call exists in the file but is never connected to the sink — must not leak false confidence onto an unrelated raw assignment.
Sanitized output passed through an unknown mutator function before the sink — the effective node at the sink is a call to that mutator, not to DOMPurify, in both implementations.
Plain string literal, statically safe.
Template literal with zero interpolations, statically safe.
Ordinary JSX children — React escapes this automatically, not an HTML sink this rule covers.
onClick is a synthetic event prop, out of scope for this rule by design.
textContent is not an HTML sink; raw input here cannot execute as markup.
createElement/appendChild/textContent never touches an HTML-sink API.
className/dataset assignment is not an HTML sink.
A real DOMPurify.sanitize() call exists but its result never reaches any HTML sink — must produce zero findings; there is no standalone 'found a sanitizer call' finding in this design.

DOMPurify reassigned to a local variable ('purifier') before use. The narrow rule intentionally does not resolve local aliases of the DOMPurify identifier itself — only verified import bindings and the literal name 'DOMPurify'. Failing safe (high) here is the objectively correct behavior for a rule that must never overclaim; this is a disclosed recall-on-recognition gap, not a vulnerability-detection failure (the finding still fires, just without the sanitizer credit).

The sanitize function reference itself is extracted into a variable and invoked at the sink as a bare call — neither implementation resolves a callee-position one-hop trace, so this is out of scope by design for both.

Destructured { sanitize } from DOMPurify, called bare. Genuinely the real function, but the narrow structural rule cannot see through a destructuring pattern back to 'DOMPurify' — a disclosed, deliberate gap; baseline recognizes this one by accident of the bare name 'sanitize' matching its identifier allowlist, which this experiment reports honestly as a case where narrowing loses a (coincidentally) correct baseline result.

A wrapper imported from another project file. Cross-file resolution is explicitly out of scope for this experiment; correct behavior is to classify as unsupported (stay high), never to silently trust it as clean.
Sanitizer used on only one branch of a ternary — the resolved initializer is a ConditionalExpression, not a bare sanitizer call, in both implementations. Correctly conservative.

DOMPurify.sanitize() is called inside a helper function; the sink calls the helper, not DOMPurify directly. Neither implementation trusts an arbitrary function's return value — correctly conservative.
Deliberately malformed JSX. Both implementations must fail to parse identically, before either rule runs. Scored separately as a parser error, never folded into TP/FP/FN.
